newsitem.title: USA: Survey shows readers buying as many, or more, books.
newsitem.headline: Survey shows readers buying as many, or more, books.

text.p: Readers are buying as many or more books than they did two years ago, countering the notion that Americans are tuning books out, said a national survey presented Friday by Publishers Weekly, a trade magazine.

"It's been assumed that readership and book buying is on the decline and that people who read a great deal and buy the most books are older, rather than younger. Our survey says that's not entirely true," magazine Editor in Chief Nora Rawlinson said at a briefing on the eve of BookExpo America, the book industry's annual convention starting Saturday in Chicago.

The survey found that, of more than 1,200 people who identified themselves as book buyers, more than half under the age of 35 said they were buying more books now than they were two years ago. Among all age groups, 41 percent said they were buying more books now than two years ago. Only 12 percent said they were buying fewer books than two years before.

Book buyers listed selection, price and location as the most important factors in choosing a bookstore. They said they decided which books to buy based mostly on friends' recommendations and authors' popularity.
Women buy more fiction than men; history leads the non-fiction sales lists; and the Bible was chosen most often as the one book people would want to have with them if stranded on a deserted island.
Market data like these, some surprising and some expected, may help the U.S. book publishing and sales industry to answer some tough questions about who, why and how people buy books.

Times are lean for many publishers and booksellers, despite evidence that reading is bigger than ever. To boost profits, bookstores are trying out coffee bars, lounges, reading clubs, tie-in product lines and other gimmicks.

Most are targeted at drawing customers into bookstores, making them feel comfortable and getting them to buy more books. And some of these strategies are working. "People really like coffee and books," Rawlinson said.
As appealing as cappucino with your Conrad may be, however, such niceties do little to address the central problem of the book business, analysts said.

"That's not where publishers are losing money. It's not in people not reading. It's not in a shortage of publishable authors," said Rudolf Hokanson, publishing analyst at the Deutsche Morgan Grenfell investment bank in New York.

Rather, analysts said, book publishing's production and distribution systems are geared to printing and shipping huge volumes of a handful of heavily promoted books with short shelf lives that may or may not sell.

If a book turns out to be a hit, the system works; if it bombs, the publisher gets swamped with unsold returns from retailers. "Except for book clubs, or a few direct marketing channels, books are not sold directly to the consumer by the publisher and the distribution system is set up with volume in mind and volume beyond the necessary requirement," Hokanson said.

To rationalise the business, publishers are trying to find ways to match production with demand more closely, while protecting relations with booksellers. Those ties are already strained, as evidenced by the BookExpo itself, which was once sponsored by the American Booksellers' Association.

As it celebrates its 50th anniversary, the convention this year is missing several major publishers, such as Simon & Schuster, Random House and Bantam Doubleday Dell. They pulled out of the show after fighting in court for two years with booksellers who had accused them of unfair pricing policies.
The legal disputes have largely been settled and the booksellers association has sold the show to a unit of Reed Elsevier, an Anglo-Dutch media company, but tension remains.

As the industry gropes for a more efficient delivery system -- whether that involves the Internet, new on-demand printing techologies or other ideas -- analysts look for little letup in the publisher-seller conflict.

"The issue is distribution and who assumes the cost and responsibility on the product," Hokanson said. "I don't think it's whether the public is reading more or less. People are reading more in general."
